title: Karp and Dimon are the CEOs who sound hawkish on China
summary: We read 1,200 statements about China by 35 CEOs and labelled each one in context. Palantir's Alex Karp and JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon lean hawkish; CEOs who sell to Chinese customers are the most conciliatory.
body_markdown:
Washington has spent two years arguing about how hard to push on China: tariffs, export controls on chips, rare-earth supply chains. The CEOs whose companies sit in the middle of that fight talk about it all the time. We took every statement about China that 35 CEOs made in interviews, podcasts and conference talks since January 2025, read each one in context, and labelled it hawkish, conciliatory or neutral.


**+31.0 and +21.1: Alex Karp and Jamie Dimon.** They are the only two CEOs on the chart whose whole 90% range sits above zero. Most of what CEOs say about China takes no side at all: 70% of the 1,200 statements are neutral.


## The hawks


**Alex Karp, Palantir** (+31.0). 15 of his 42 China statements are hawkish and 2 are conciliatory. Karp frames China as the other side of a two-player contest: "This is a have-have-not world. It's going to be either us or them basically deciding the world order" ([April 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bkIpvbZpXDg&t=787s) ).


**Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan Chase** (+21.1). Dimon argues for cutting supply-chain dependence: "a barrier, that we will not import rare earths from China. And we have to do it quick" ([May 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SDkEwjyset4&t=450s) ). He is not one-sided. 9 of his 95 statements are conciliatory, such as "I don't think they have to be a natural enemy of ours" ([Economic Club of Chicago, October 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UkvigLsQ2Ic&t=1432s) ).


**Jim Farley, Ford** (+10.2). Farley talks about China as a competitive threat: "the competitive threat from China especially really requires a complete reinvention" ([Automotive News, September 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb-J_UELubE&t=597s) ). He also praises Chinese carmakers often, so his range (−1.0 to +29.4) reaches zero and we do not call him a hawk with confidence.


## The most conciliatory


**Joanne Crevoiserat, Tapestry** (−65.0). 13 of her 20 statements are conciliatory and none are hawkish. "I believe that China can be our fastest growing market over the next five years" ([CGTN, April 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sRNzU1ikTxs&t=707s) ).


**Brian Niccol, Starbucks** (−44.6). "We do believe China is a tremendous growth market" ([Bloomberg, January 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=daRfE6AzmYY&t=799s) ).


**Jane Fraser, Citi** (−37.2). Fraser argues for stability: "China's a very important partner of the US from a trading point of view" ([Council on Foreign Relations, June 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LYDEnLIs858&t=1190s) ).


**Jensen Huang, Nvidia** (−28.6). Huang has the most China statements of anyone (147). He is the loudest critic of US export controls: "I completely disagree that we should ban China of all American products" ([CBS Sunday Morning, September 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xCUala5j7aQ&t=1300s) ).


**Elon Musk, Tesla** (−12.7). Musk mostly praises Chinese manufacturing: "China just has a very strong inherent ability to do manufacturing well" ([CGTN, September 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jrUNnrcmFCU&t=80s) ).


The pattern: CEOs who sell to Chinese consumers or companies (Tapestry, Starbucks, Citi, Nvidia, the miners) talk about China as an opportunity. The CEOs who lean hawkish sell to the Pentagon, compete with Chinese exporters, or worry about where critical supplies come from.


## Methodology


**Source.** FactIQ's media-appearance statements: things executives said in TV interviews, podcasts and conference talks, each stored with the speaker's exact words, the date and a timestamped link. Earnings calls are not included.


**Which statements.** Every statement by a company executive that mentions China (china, chinese, beijing, CCP or Xi Jinping) in an appearance published between 2025-01-09 and 2026-11-06. We kept sitting CEOs of companies based outside mainland China who had at least 15 such statements, and merged different spellings of the same name. The same quote is often recorded twice, for example when one interview is published in two places, so each quote counts once per CEO. That left 1,200 statements by 35 CEOs.


**Labelling.** A word list cannot tell which side a speaker is on: "export controls" is hawkish from someone who wants them and conciliatory from someone arguing against them. So each statement was read in context and given one label, hawkish, conciliatory or neutral, by an AI model (Claude Haiku) following the written rubric below. The model saw the quote, a one-line summary of it, the speaker and the appearance, in shuffled order, five statements at a time.


**Two passes.** Every statement that received a stance in the first pass was labelled again by a second, independent pass that could not see the first label. To keep the second pass honest, 300 statements the first pass called neutral were mixed in. A statement counts as hawkish or conciliatory only when both passes agree; otherwise it is neutral. The two passes gave the same label 82% of the time (Cohen's kappa 0.72), and in only 2 of 842 cases did one say hawkish and the other conciliatory.


**Check against a blind sample.** A separate, more capable model (Claude Fable) labelled a random 100 statements with the same rubric before seeing any of the Haiku labels. The final labels match that sample on 93% (kappa 0.82), with no case of hawkish against conciliatory. After the first pass alone the match was 80%: the model was too quick to read a stance into plain business facts. We tightened the rubric's definition of neutral before the second pass, which is why the second pass uses the longer rubric.


**Scoring.** Net hawkishness = the share of a CEO's China statements labelled hawkish minus the share labelled conciliatory, in percentage points. Neutral statements count in the denominator, so a CEO who mostly reports sales figures scores near zero.


**Uncertainty.** The 90% range comes from resampling each CEO's appearances 4,000 times. We resample whole appearances, not single statements, because ten statements from one interview are not ten independent observations.


**What is on the chart.** The 18 CEOs with at least 20 China statements across at least 3 appearances. The table below has all 35.


**Limits.** No human coded these statements. The labels come from one AI model and the blind check from another, so the two can share blind spots. About 7 in 100 labels would be disputed. Most CEOs have few statements with a stance (356 of 1,200 overall), so the ranges are wide and neighbours on the chart should not be ranked against each other. A statement is judged on its own; an interview's overall argument can differ. Coverage depends on which appearances FactIQ has recorded.


### The rubric


```text
# Labelling rubric: a CEO's stance toward China


Each item is one statement made by a company CEO in an interview, podcast or conference talk.
`quote` is what they said. `summary` restates it in context. Label the stance toward China that
THE SPEAKER expresses in that statement. "China" means the Chinese government, the Chinese
economy or market, or Chinese companies.


Give each statement exactly one label:


**hawkish** - the speaker treats China as an adversary, a threat, or a rival that has to be
countered or beaten. Includes:
- warning that China (or Chinese companies) is a danger to their country, industry or company;
- saying dependence on China is a risk that must be reduced (reshoring, decoupling, new supply chains);
- supporting or calling for tariffs, export controls, bans or other restrictions aimed at China;
- accusing China of unfair conduct (theft, subsidies, dumping, coercion, spying);
- "we must win the race against China" framing.


**conciliatory** - the speaker treats China as a partner, an opportunity, or a relationship worth
keeping. Includes:
- describing China as an attractive or important market, customer base or source of talent,
with commitment to being there;
- calling for engagement, dialogue, cooperation, stability or trust between the countries;
- arguing AGAINST tariffs, export controls, decoupling or other restrictions on China;
- praising China, Chinese companies or Chinese partners without presenting them as a threat.


**neutral** - no stance toward China. Includes:
- plain business reporting: sales, volumes, prices, market share, forecasts, operations in China;
- describing a policy, an event or someone else's position without endorsing or opposing it;
- factual statements about what China or Chinese companies do or have, with no judgment;
- China is mentioned only in passing, or the statement is not really about China.


## Rules


1. Judge the meaning in context, never single words. "Export controls" is hawkish when the
speaker supports them, conciliatory when the speaker argues against them, and neutral when
the speaker only describes their effect on the business.
2. Label the speaker's own view. If they report what a government or a competitor thinks
without agreeing or disagreeing, that is neutral.
3. Describing strong Chinese competition is hawkish only if it is framed as a threat or
something that must be countered. Admiring it, or stating it as fact, is conciliatory or neutral.
4. Saying sales in China fell or rose is neutral. Saying China is a great market the company
is committed to is conciliatory.
5. When a statement really carries no stance, or you cannot tell, choose neutral. Do not force a stance.


## Statements that are neutral, even though they mention China


Most statements carry no stance. These are all neutral:
- Reporting numbers or facts about the business in China: units sold, revenue, number of sites,
stores, partners or customers, an investment amount, how long the company has been there.
(It becomes conciliatory only when the speaker adds an explicit judgment such as "investing in
China is the right decision" or "China is a very important market for us".)
- Comparing China with the US or other countries on size, speed, cost, energy or output,
without saying what should be done about it.
- Saying a company or industry has to "compete with China" as a plain fact of business,
without calling China a threat or calling for action against it.
- Describing what customers, governments or other companies are doing about China
(for example moving supply chains) without endorsing or opposing it.
- Listing China as one item among several risks, markets or countries.
- Forecasts about what China or Chinese companies will do next, stated without alarm or approval.
```


### Query


```text
SELECT c.claim_id, c.speaker, c.primary_ticker, c.canonical_statement, c.verbatim_quote,
c.start_s, a.video_id, a.url, a.title, a.channel, a.published_at
FROM transcripts.appearance_claims c
JOIN transcripts.appearances a USING (video_id)
WHERE c.speaker_role = 'exec'
AND c.primary_ticker IS NOT NULL AND c.primary_ticker <> ''
AND a.published_at >= DATE '2025-01-01'
AND c.search_tsv @@ to_tsquery('english', 'china | chines | beij | ccp | xi<->jinp');
```


### Scoring


```text
# labels: one row per statement, with the stance from each of the two passes
def final_stance(first_pass, second_pass):
# a statement gets a stance only when both passes give it the same one
if first_pass != "neutral" and first_pass == second_pass:
return first_pass
return "neutral"


def net_hawkishness(statements):
hawkish = sum(s["stance"] == "hawkish" for s in statements)
conciliatory = sum(s["stance"] == "conciliatory" for s in statements)
return 100 * (hawkish - conciliatory) / len(statements)


def interval(statements, draws=4000):
# resample whole appearances, because statements from one interview move together
by_appearance = group_by(statements, key="video_id")
scores = sorted(
net_hawkishness(flatten(random.choices(by_appearance, k=len(by_appearance))))
for _ in range(draws)
)
return scores[int(0.05 * draws)], scores[int(0.95 * draws)]
```
